questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes an agent that disrupts prenatal development; what is it called?
questions.explanation: A teratogen is an agent that can disrupt prenatal development and cause malformations. Nutrients and hormones support rather than disrupt development.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes a window when a skill must develop or be lost; what is this?

options.text: A critical period with strict timing

questions.explanation: A critical period is a strict window when a skill must develop or be permanently impaired. Sensitive periods are more flexible.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes a newborn prefers a story read during pregnancy; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses prenatal learning with postnatal imprinting

questions.explanation: Prenatal auditory learning occurs when fetuses learn sounds heard in utero, shown by newborn preferences. It is distinct from postnatal imprinting.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician recommends skin-to-skin contact for a premature infant; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses contact care with light treatment
confuses contact care with tube feeding

questions.explanation: Kangaroo care involves skin-to-skin contact between parent and premature infant, supporting bonding and regulation. Other practices address different needs.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Design a study to test whether a prenatal agent affects infant motor development.

answer.exemplar: Randomly assign pregnant participants to exposed and unexposed groups, control for confounds, then compare infant motor scores at six months with blinded assessors.

questions.explanation: A valid design requires randomization, control of confounds, and blinded outcome assessment to isolate the agent's effect on motor development.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician expects independent walking around what age?
questions.explanation: Independent walking typically emerges around 12 months. Sitting occurs earlier, and running develops later.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician touches an infant's cheek and the head turns toward it; what reflex?
questions.explanation: The rooting reflex turns the head toward a touch on the cheek, aiding feeding. The Moro reflex is a startle response.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes an infant searching for a hidden toy; what concept emerges?
questions.explanation: Object permanence is understanding that objects exist when out of sight. Conservation and egocentrism are later Piagetian concepts.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes an infant briefly holding a location in mind; what capacity?

options.misconception: confuses brief holding with long-term storage
confuses active holding with sensory buffer

questions.explanation: Working memory briefly holds and manipulates information. In infancy it is limited but present, supporting tasks like object permanence.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes a child judges quantity unchanged after pouring; what concept?
questions.explanation: Conservation is understanding that quantity remains the same despite changes in appearance. Object permanence concerns hidden objects.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician asks when teratogen exposure is most harmful; what is the answer?
questions.explanation: Teratogens are most harmful during organogenesis in the first trimester, when organs form. Later exposure has different effects.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician notes vision must develop in infancy or be impaired; what principle?
questions.explanation: Vision has a critical period in infancy; deprivation during this window can cause lasting impairment. Sensitive periods allow more recovery.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Does prenatal auditory learning imply full language acquisition before birth?
questions.explanation: Prenatal auditory learning supports sound preferences, not full language acquisition. Grammar and vocabulary develop postnatally.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Is kangaroo care beneficial beyond bonding?
questions.explanation: Kangaroo care supports bonding and also stabilizes heart rate, temperature, and breathing. It complements rather than replaces medical care.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A study shows 5 percent malformation in exposed infants versus 2 percent in controls; what is the excess risk?

options.misconception: reports control rate instead of excess
reports exposed rate instead of excess

questions.explanation: Subtracting the control rate (2 percent) from the exposed rate (5 percent) gives 3 percentage points excess risk. Addition would be incorrect.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Order gross motor milestones from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Typical order is sitting, then crawling, then walking. Each builds on prior motor control and strength.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Should primitive reflexes persist beyond infancy?
questions.explanation: Primitive reflexes typically integrate during infancy as voluntary control develops. Persistence may indicate neurological concerns.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: An infant searches for a toy hidden under a cloth; what does this show?
questions.explanation: Searching for a hidden toy demonstrates object permanence, understanding objects exist out of sight. Conservation concerns quantity changes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Is infant working memory as large as adult working memory?
questions.explanation: Infant working memory is more limited than adult working memory, though present. It grows with maturation and experience.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A child says water amount is same after pouring into a taller glass; what concept?
questions.explanation: Judging quantity unchanged after a perceptual transformation demonstrates conservation. Object permanence concerns hidden objects.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician lists alcohol as a prenatal risk agent; what category?
questions.explanation: Alcohol is a teratogen that can disrupt prenatal development. It is not a nutrient or hormone.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician contrasts strict versus flexible developmental windows; which is critical?
questions.explanation: Critical periods are strict windows; sensitive periods are more flexible. The distinction matters for intervention timing.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A newborn calms to a lullaby played during pregnancy; what explains this?

options.misconception: confuses prenatal learning with postnatal imprinting
confuses prenatal learning with postnatal habituation

questions.explanation: Calming to a prenatal sound indicates auditory learning before birth. Postnatal imprinting and habituation are different processes.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician places a premature infant in a controlled warmth device; what is this?
questions.explanation: An incubator provides controlled warmth and environment for premature infants. Kangaroo care is skin-to-skin contact.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a clinician ethically tests teratogenic effects in humans.

answer.exemplar: Clinicians rely on observational studies and existing exposure data rather than experiments, comparing outcomes while controlling confounds to avoid harming fetuses.

questions.explanation: Ethical constraints prohibit experimental teratogen exposure in humans, so clinicians use observational designs with careful control of confounding variables.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: If sitting emerges at 6 months and walking at 12 months, how many months apart?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 6 from 12 gives 6 months between sitting and walking. This is a typical gross motor interval.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A clinician startles an infant and sees arm extension then embrace; what reflex?
questions.explanation: The Moro reflex is a startle response with arm extension and embrace. Rooting is a feeding reflex triggered by cheek touch.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Does object permanence emerge suddenly or gradually?
questions.explanation: Object permanence develops gradually during infancy, not suddenly. Piaget placed full achievement later, but partial forms appear earlier.

options.misconception: confuses brief holding with long-term storage
confuses active holding with sensory buffer

questions.explanation: Working memory briefly holds the location, supporting search for hidden objects. Long-term memory would not explain brief holding.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Does conservation develop before or after object permanence?
questions.explanation: Conservation develops after object permanence, typically in the concrete operational stage. Object permanence emerges in infancy.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why teratogens are most dangerous during organogenesis.

answer.exemplar: During organogenesis organs form rapidly, so teratogens can disrupt cell differentiation and cause structural malformations that later exposure rarely produces.

questions.explanation: Rapid organ formation during the first trimester makes tissues vulnerable to teratogenic disruption, leading to structural defects.

questions.stem: A clinician intervenes early for congenital vision loss; why early?

options.text: Critical period for vision is early

questions.explanation: The critical period for vision is early in infancy, so intervention must occur before it closes to prevent lasting impairment.

questions.stem: Prenatal auditory learning differs from postnatal imprinting in that it?

options.misconception: confuses auditory learning with motor learning

questions.explanation: Prenatal auditory learning occurs before birth, whereas postnatal imprinting occurs after birth. Timing distinguishes them.

questions.stem: An odds ratio of 2.0 for malformation means exposed infants have?
questions.explanation: An odds ratio of 2.0 means the exposed group has twice the odds of malformation compared to controls. It does not imply zero or unchanged risk.

questions.explanation: The grasp reflex closes the hand around an object placed in the palm. Rooting is triggered by cheek touch.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why confound control matters in teratogen studies.

answer.exemplar: Confound control matters because maternal health, nutrition, and age can also affect outcomes, so uncontrolled comparisons may falsely attribute effects to the agent.

questions.explanation: Without controlling confounds, observed associations may reflect alternative causes rather than teratogenic effects.

questions.stem: Does full object permanence require memory beyond infancy?

options.text: No, it is complete at birth

questions.explanation: Object permanence develops through infancy as memory and cognition mature. It is not present at birth or delayed to adulthood.

questions.explanation: Working memory briefly holds information for immediate use, supporting early learning. It does not store facts permanently or create reflexes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why conservation develops after object permanence.

answer.exemplar: Conservation requires decentering from a single perceptual dimension, a capacity that matures after infants first understand objects persist when hidden.

questions.explanation: Conservation builds on earlier cognitive achievements like object permanence and requires the ability to consider multiple dimensions simultaneously.
